title: Security Shared-Responsibility Model
readerIntent: Understand which security controls Nodics provides and which controls remain with the deploying organization, partner, and operator.
owner: Shared across Nodics capability owners, customer projects, deployment operators, cloud/provider controls, and business governance
summary: Nodics provides security contracts and fail-closed controls, while every deployment remains responsible for correct configuration, infrastructure, access governance, monitoring, evidence, legal obligations, and incident response.

sections.heading: Nodics provides
items: Separate human, customer, service, scheduled-process, API-key, and refresh-session credential contracts.
Tenant-aware authentication, token class/audience, permission, route exposure, schema action, field masking, record ownership, validation, and audit extension points.
Layered configuration and customization without requiring customer-specific framework forks.
Governed runtime preview, approval, activation, audit, and rollback for eligible policies.
Provider-neutral contracts, safe errors, observability dimensions, migration controls, and verification suites.

sections.heading: Customer and implementation partner responsibilities
items: Classify data and threats; design tenants, enterprises, roles, permissions, ownership, retention, residency, consent, and regulatory controls.
Keep customer business rules in project modules and preserve Nodics authority boundaries when customizing.
Review third-party libraries and providers, qualify integrations, protect credentials, and maintain secure dependency/update practices.
Test project-specific authorization, abuse cases, privacy, workflows, data movement, clients, and integrations.
Maintain accurate end-user, administrator, developer, security, and recovery documentation.

sections.heading: Deployment and operations responsibilities
items: Provide supported runtime versions, TLS, certificates, DNS, network segmentation, gateway/WAF/rate limits, secret management, encryption keys, provider hardening, backups, restore, and disaster recovery.
Configure strong secrets, strict distributed session state, exact browser origins, secure cookies, least privilege, disabled unnecessary exposure, and production-safe compatibility settings.
Monitor, alert, retain audit evidence, review access, rotate credentials, patch dependencies, rehearse recovery, and operate incident response.
Validate the real production-like topology and providers; a passing local MonoServer test is not production certification.

sections.heading: Decision-maker questions
items: Who owns each dataset, access decision, provider, deployment, and incident?
Which evidence demonstrates tenant isolation, least privilege, resilience, recovery, privacy, and regulatory compliance?
Which compatibility or local-development exceptions remain enabled, and who approved their removal plan?
How quickly can credentials be revoked, affected principals identified, service restored, and customers notified?

sections.heading: Complete guide: Security Shared-Responsibility Model
paragraphs: This guide helps business owners, project teams, platform operators, providers, and auditors agree who must protect what. A secure framework cannot compensate for missing production secrets, open networks, unprotected backups, or absent operational ownership.

sections.heading: Beginner View
paragraphs: Think of Nodics as a secure building design.
Every layer must do its part.
items: Nodics supplies doors, locks, room boundaries, access rules, alarms, and
The project decides who receives access and how the building is customized.
Infrastructure operates the site, network, keys, backups, and monitoring.
The business decides which information is sensitive and which rules apply.

sections.heading: Responsibility Matrix
paragraphs:
| Area | Nodics framework | Customer/project | Infrastructure/provider | Business/security organization |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Identity model | Human, service, API-key, permission, group, tenant, and token contracts | Connect selected IAM/CIAM and define project identities | Protect identity-provider availability and transport | Approve identity lifecycle and access policy |
| Authorization | Route permissions, token-type boundaries, service checks | Assign least-privilege roles and project permissions | Enforce gateway/mesh identity where selected | Approve roles, segregation of duties, reviews |
| Tenant isolation | Tenant-aware route, service, data, cache, search, job, import, and event contracts | Choose tenant model and prove custom code preserves it | Provide isolated storage/network where required | Classify customers and residency requirements |
| Secrets | Governed secret inputs, insecure-default rejection, redaction | Supply and rotate real secrets outside source control | Operate secret manager/KMS/HSM if selected | Set rotation and emergency-access policy |
| API security | Authentication pipeline, permissions, exposure gates, CORS, headers, limits, rate policy | Enable only required API categories and origins | TLS, WAF, gateway, DDoS, certificate lifecycle | Define external exposure and abuse objectives |
| Data protection | Validation, exact ownership, access policy, safe projections | Classify fields and add project-specific controls | Encryption at rest/in transit, storage access, backup protection | Retention, deletion, privacy, legal basis |
| Runtime change | Preview, approval, activation, audit, rollback capabilities | Configure approvers and protected environments | Preserve audit storage and deployment separation | Define change authority and emergency process |
| Logging/diagnostics | Central redaction and sanitized diagnostic contracts | Avoid logging project secrets or sensitive payloads | Secure collection, retention, access, alerting | Approve retention and investigation access |
| Resilience | Bounded retry, circuit, readiness, cache and topology contracts | Select policies for business criticality | Operate redundant providers and capacity | Define SLO, RTO, RPO, crisis priorities |
| Testing/release | Security, route, tenant, topology, generated, and release gates | Add project and customer-specific misuse tests | Run gates in controlled CI/CD | Approve acceptance evidence and exceptions |
| Vulnerabilities | Dependency ownership and supported runtime contract | Track project dependencies and remediation | Patch hosts, images, databases, brokers, gateways | Set risk acceptance and disclosure process |
| Compliance | Evidence-producing capabilities | Configure solution-specific controls | Supply provider attestations | Own legal interpretation and certification |

sections.heading: Required Production Decisions
paragraphs: Before production, record owners and evidence for:
items: Identity provider and break-glass administration.
Secret source, rotation, revocation, and recovery.
Public, partner, internal, and administration network boundaries.
Tenant placement and any dedicated database, search, cache, or messaging
TLS termination and trust between gateway, servers, and modules.
Log, audit, and security-event retention.
Backup encryption, restore testing, RTO, and RPO.
Dependency and container/host patching.
Vulnerability reporting, triage, remediation, and disclosure.
Release approval, rollback authority, and emergency change.
Incident detection, containment, evidence preservation, and notification.
Provider qualification and failure behavior.

sections.heading: Fail-Safe Configuration Rules

Do not use local sample credentials or source-controlled secrets.
Do not make an internal route public to solve connectivity.

sections.heading: Operational Review Cadence
paragraphs:
| Frequency | Review |
| --- | --- |
| Every release | Dependency changes, route exposure, permissions, generated contracts, security tests, rollback plan |
| Monthly or risk-based | Privileged access, inactive accounts, secret age, provider health, alert quality |
| Quarterly or policy-defined | Tenant isolation evidence, restore exercise, incident exercise, provider and runtime maturity |
| After an incident or major change | Threat assumptions, access paths, logs, detection gaps, recovery evidence, documentation |
